Chapter 4 · Economics · Understanding Economic Development

Globalisation and the Indian Economy

In a matter of years our markets have been transformed. This chapter explains how MNCs spread production across countries, how foreign trade integrates markets, what technology and liberalisation have to do with it, what the WTO does — and who gains and who loses from globalisation.

01

Chapter Overview

What this chapter is about, at a glance

As consumers in today’s world, some of us have a wide choice of goods and services. The latest models of digital cameras, mobile phones and televisions made by the leading manufacturers of the world are within our reach; every season new models of automobiles appear on Indian roads. Gone are the days when Ambassador and Fiat were the only cars on Indian roads. Such wide-ranging choice is a relatively recent phenomenon — you would not have found such variety even two decades back.

How do we understand these rapid transformations? The chapter answers through four connected ideas. First, production across countries: multinational corporations (MNCs) set up offices and factories where they can get cheap labour and other resources, so that costs are low and profits greater. Second, foreign trade and integration of markets: goods travel between markets, choice rises, prices of similar goods tend to equalise, and producers in different countries compete.

Third, what globalisation is and what has enabled it: rapid integration between countries, driven by technology — especially transport and information and communication technology — and by liberalisation of foreign trade and investment policy since 1991, with the WTO pressing for free trade.

Finally, the impact: consumers, skilled workers and large Indian companies have gained; small producers and many workers have been hit hard. The chapter ends with the struggle for a fair globalisation — opportunities for all, with the benefits shared better.

MNC

A company that owns or controls production in more than one nation.

Investment

Money spent to buy assets such as land, building, machines and other equipment. Investment by MNCs is called foreign investment.

Globalisation

The process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries.

Trade barrier

A restriction set up by the government to regulate foreign trade — a tax on imports, or a quota.

Liberalisation

Removing barriers or restrictions set by the government. India began this in 1991.

WTO

World Trade Organisation — aims to liberalise international trade; about 160 member countries; started at the initiative of developed countries.

SEZ

Special Economic Zone — an industrial zone with world-class facilities where units pay no taxes for the first five years.

Fair globalisation

Globalisation that creates opportunities for all and ensures that its benefits are shared better.

Production Across Countries

Until the middle of the twentieth century, production was largely organised within countries. What crossed the boundaries of these countries were raw material, foodstuff and finished products. Colonies such as India exported raw materials and foodstuff and imported finished goods. Trade was the main channel connecting distant countries. This was before large companies called multinational corporations (MNCs) emerged on the scene.

Definition

MNC: a company that owns or controls production in more than one nation. MNCs set up offices and factories for production in regions where they can get cheap labour and other resources — so that the cost of production is low and the MNCs can earn greater profits.

Source extract

Spreading of production by an MNC: a large MNC producing industrial equipment designs its products in research centres in the United States, and then has the components manufactured in China. These are then shipped to Mexico and Eastern Europe where the products are assembled, and the finished products are sold all over the world. Meanwhile, the company’s customer care is carried out through call centres located in India.

In this example the MNC is not only selling its finished products globally, but — more important — the goods and services are produced globally. Production is organised in increasingly complex ways: the process is divided into small parts and spread out across the globe. China provides the advantage of being a cheap manufacturing location; Mexico and Eastern Europe are useful for their closeness to the markets in the US and Europe; India has highly skilled engineers who can understand the technical aspects of production, and educated English-speaking youth who can provide customer care. And all this can mean 50–60 per cent cost-savings for the MNC.

How do MNCs set up production?

At times MNCs set up production jointly with some of the local companies of these countries. The benefit to the local company is two-fold: MNCs can provide money for additional investments, like buying new machines for faster production, and they might bring with them the latest technology for production.

In general, MNCs set up production where it is close to the markets; where there is skilled and unskilled labour available at low costs; and where the availability of other factors of production is assured. In addition, MNCs might look for government policies that look after their interests.

Definition

Investment: the money that is spent to buy assets such as land, building, machines and other equipment. Investment made by MNCs is called foreign investment. Any investment is made with the hope that these assets will earn profits.

Interlinking Production Across Countries

But the most common route for MNC investments is to buy up local companies and then to expand production. MNCs with huge wealth can quite easily do so. Cargill Foods, a very large American MNC, has bought over smaller Indian companies such as Parakh Foods. Parakh Foods had built a large marketing network in various parts of India, where its brand was well reputed, and had four oil refineries, whose control has now shifted to Cargill. Cargill is now the largest producer of edible oil in India, with a capacity to make 5 million pouches daily.

In fact, many of the top MNCs have wealth exceeding the entire budgets of the developing country governments. With such enormous wealth, imagine the power and influence of these MNCs.

There is another way in which MNCs control production. Large MNCs in developed countries place orders for production with small producers. Garments, footwear and sports items are examples of industries where production is carried out by a large number of small producers around the world. The products are supplied to the MNCs, which then sell these under their own brand names to customers. These large MNCs have tremendous power to determine price, quality, delivery and labour conditions for these distant producers.

Thus MNCs are spreading production and interacting with local producers in various countries in a variety of ways: by setting up partnerships with local companies, by using local companies for supplies, by closely competing with local companies, or by buying them up. As a result, production in widely dispersed locations is getting interlinked.

Ford Motors — a case of interlinking

Source extract

Ford Motors, an American company, is one of the world’s largest automobile manufacturers, with production spread over 26 countries. Ford Motors came to India in 1995 and spent Rs 1,700 crore to set up a large plant near Chennai. This was done in collaboration with Mahindra and Mahindra, a major Indian manufacturer of jeeps and trucks. By 2017 Ford Motors was selling 88,000 cars in the Indian markets, while another 1,81,000 cars were exported from India to South Africa, Mexico, Brazil and the United States of America. In recent years, Ford stopped producing cars for selling in India but exports cars and car engines on a small scale to other countries.

Foreign Trade and Integration of Markets

For a long time foreign trade has been the main channel connecting countries. In history you would have read about the trade routes connecting India and South Asia to markets both in the East and West, and of the trading interests which attracted companies such as the East India Company to India.

What is the basic function of foreign trade? Foreign trade creates an opportunity for producers to reach beyond the domestic markets — markets of their own countries. Producers can sell their produce not only within the country but can also compete in markets located in other countries. Similarly, for buyers, import of goods produced in another country is one way of expanding the choice of goods beyond what is domestically produced.

Chinese toys in India

Chinese manufacturers learn of an opportunity to export toys to India, where toys are sold at a high price. They start exporting plastic toys to India. Buyers in India now have the option of choosing between Indian and Chinese toys. Because of the cheaper prices and new designs, Chinese toys become more popular in the Indian markets. Within a year, 70 to 80 per cent of the toy shops have replaced Indian toys with Chinese toys. Toys are now cheaper in the Indian markets than earlier.

What is happening here? As a result of trade, Chinese toys come into the Indian markets. In the competition between Indian and Chinese toys, Chinese toys prove better. Indian buyers have a greater choice of toys and at lower prices; for the Chinese toy makers this provides an opportunity to expand business. The opposite is true for Indian toy makers, who face losses as their toys sell much less.

In general, with the opening of trade, goods travel from one market to another, the choice of goods rises, prices of similar goods in the two markets tend to become equal, and producers in the two countries now closely compete against each other even though they are separated by thousands of miles. Foreign trade thus results in connecting the markets, or integration of markets, in different countries.

What is Globalisation?

In the past two to three decades, more and more MNCs have been looking for locations around the world which would be cheap for their production. Foreign investment by MNCs in these countries has been rising, and at the same time foreign trade between countries has been rising rapidly. A large part of the foreign trade is also controlled by MNCs — for instance, the car manufacturing plant of Ford Motors in India not only produces cars for the Indian markets, it also exports cars to other developing countries and exports car components for its many factories around the world. Likewise, the activities of most MNCs involve substantial trade in goods and also in services.

Definition

Globalisation is the process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries. The result of greater foreign investment and greater foreign trade has been greater integration of production and markets across countries. MNCs are playing a major role in the globalisation process: more and more goods and services, investments and technology are moving between countries, and most regions of the world are in closer contact with each other than a few decades back.

Besides the movement of goods, services, investments and technology, there is one more way in which countries can be connected — the movement of people between countries. People usually move in search of better income, better jobs or better education. In the past few decades, however, there has not been much increase in the movement of people between countries due to various restrictions.

Factors That Have Enabled Globalisation

Technology

Rapid improvement in technology has been one major factor that has stimulated the globalisation process. In the past fifty years there have been several improvements in transportation technology, making much faster delivery of goods across long distances possible at lower costs.

Containers for transport of goods have been a major breakthrough: goods are placed in containers that can be loaded intact onto ships, railways, planes and trucks. Containers have led to a huge reduction in port handling costs and increased the speed with which exports can reach markets. Similarly, the cost of air transport has fallen, enabling much greater volumes of goods to be transported by airlines.

Even more remarkable have been the developments in information and communication technology. In recent times, technology in the areas of telecommunications, computers and the internet has been changing rapidly. Telecommunication facilities — telegraph, telephone including mobile phones, fax — are used to contact one another around the world, to access information instantly and to communicate from remote areas, facilitated by satellite communication devices. Computers have entered almost every field of activity, and the internet allows us to obtain and share information on almost anything, send instant electronic mail and talk across the world at negligible costs.

Source extract

Using IT in globalisation: a news magazine published for London readers is to be designed and printed in Delhi. The text is sent through the internet to the Delhi office; the designers get orders on how to design the magazine from the office in London using telecommunication facilities. The designing is done on a computer; after printing, the magazines are sent by air to London. Even the payment for designing and printing, from a bank in London to a bank in Delhi, is done instantly through the internet (e-banking).

Information and communication technology (IT) has played a major role in spreading out production of services across countries. A large part of this revolution is about the ability to digitise information — text, sound and images — and send it across the world in seconds at almost no cost.

Liberalisation of foreign trade and foreign investment policy

Let us return to the example of imports of Chinese toys in India. Suppose the Indian government puts a tax on import of toys. Those who wish to import these toys would have to pay tax, so buyers would have to pay a higher price and Chinese toys would no longer be as cheap; imports would automatically reduce and Indian toy-makers would prosper.

Definition

Trade barrier: a tax on imports is an example. It is called a barrier because some restriction has been set up. Governments can use trade barriers to increase or decrease (regulate) foreign trade and to decide what kinds of goods, and how much of each, should come into the country.

The Indian government, after Independence, had put barriers to foreign trade and foreign investment. This was considered necessary to protect the producers within the country from foreign competition: industries were just coming up in the 1950s and 1960s, and competition from imports at that stage would not have allowed these industries to come up. Thus India allowed imports of only essential items such as machinery, fertilisers and petroleum. Note that all developed countries, during the early stages of development, have given protection to domestic producers through a variety of means.

Starting around 1991, some far-reaching changes in policy were made in India. The government decided that the time had come for Indian producers to compete with producers around the globe, and felt that competition would improve their performance since they would have to improve quality. This decision was supported by powerful international organisations. Thus barriers on foreign trade and foreign investment were removed to a large extent, meaning goods could be imported and exported easily and foreign companies could set up factories and offices here.

Removing barriers or restrictions set by the government is what is known as liberalisation. With liberalisation of trade, businesses are allowed to make decisions freely about what they wish to import or export; the government imposes much less restriction than before and is therefore said to be more liberal.

World Trade Organisation

We have seen that the liberalisation of foreign trade and investment in India was supported by some very powerful international organisations. These organisations say that all barriers to foreign trade and investment are harmful, there should be no barriers, and trade between countries should be “free”; all countries should liberalise their policies.

The World Trade Organisation (WTO) is one such organisation whose aim is to liberalise international trade. Started at the initiative of the developed countries, the WTO establishes rules regarding international trade and sees that these rules are obeyed. About 160 countries of the world are currently members.

Though the WTO is supposed to allow free trade for all, in practice it is seen that the developed countries have unfairly retained trade barriers. On the other hand, WTO rules have forced the developing countries to remove trade barriers. An example of this is the current debate on trade in agricultural products.

Source extract

Debate on trade practices: developing countries are asking the developed country governments, “We have reduced trade barriers as per WTO rules. But you have ignored the rules of WTO and have continued to pay your farmers vast sums of money. You have asked our governments to stop supporting our farmers, but you are doing so yourselves. Is this free and fair trade?”

In the US, the share of agriculture in GDP is only 1 per cent and its share in total employment a tiny 0.5 per cent. Yet this very small percentage of people engaged in agriculture receive massive sums of money from the US government for production and for exports. Because of this money, US farmers can sell farm products at abnormally low prices, and the surplus is sold in other countries’ markets at low prices, adversely affecting farmers there.

Impact of Globalisation in India

In the last twenty years, globalisation of the Indian economy has come a long way. What has been its effect on people’s lives? Let us look at the evidence.

For consumers

Globalisation and greater competition among producers — both local and foreign — has been of advantage to consumers, particularly the well-off sections in urban areas. There is greater choice before these consumers, who now enjoy improved quality and lower prices for several products, and as a result enjoy much higher standards of living than was possible earlier.

For producers and workers — not uniform

Among producers and workers the impact has not been uniform.

  1. MNCs have increased their investments in India over the past 20 years, which means investing in India has been beneficial for them. They have been interested in industries such as cell phones, automobiles, electronics, soft drinks, fast food, and services such as banking in urban areas, because these products have a large number of well-off buyers. In these industries and services, new jobs have been created, and local companies supplying raw materials have prospered.
  2. Several of the top Indian companies have been able to benefit from increased competition. They have invested in newer technology and production methods and raised their production standards; some have gained from successful collaborations with foreign companies.
  3. Globalisation has enabled some large Indian companies to emerge as multinationals themselves — Tata Motors (automobiles), Infosys (IT), Ranbaxy (medicines), Asian Paints (paints) and Sundaram Fasteners (nuts and bolts) are some Indian companies spreading their operations worldwide.
  4. Globalisation has also created new opportunities for companies providing services, particularly those involving IT. The Indian company producing a magazine for a London-based company, and call centres, are examples. A host of services — data entry, accounting, administrative tasks, engineering — are now done cheaply in countries such as India and exported to developed countries.

Steps to attract foreign investment

In recent years the central and state governments are taking special steps to attract foreign companies to invest in India. Industrial zones called Special Economic Zones (SEZs) are being set up. SEZs are to have world-class facilities: electricity, water, roads, transport, storage, recreational and educational facilities. Companies who set up production units in the SEZs do not have to pay taxes for an initial period of five years.

The government has also allowed flexibility in the labour laws to attract foreign investment. Companies in the organised sector have to obey rules that protect workers’ rights, but in recent years the government has allowed companies to ignore many of these. Instead of hiring workers on a regular basis, companies hire workers “flexibly” for short periods when there is intense pressure of work, to reduce the cost of labour. However, still not satisfied, foreign companies are demanding more flexibility in labour laws.

Small Producers — Compete or Perish

For a large number of small producers and workers, globalisation has posed major challenges. Batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys, tyres, dairy products and vegetable oil are some examples of industries where small manufacturers have been hit hard due to competition. Several of the units have shut down, rendering many workers jobless. The small and medium industries in India employ the largest number of workers — 11 crores — in the country, next only to agriculture.

Case study

Ravi’s story: Ravi took a loan from a bank to start his own company producing capacitors in 1992 in Hosur, an industrial town in Tamil Nadu. Capacitors are used in many electronic home appliances including tube lights and televisions. Within three years he expanded production and had 20 workers. His struggle started when the government removed restrictions on imports of capacitors as per its agreement at the WTO in 2001. His main clients, the television companies, used to buy capacitors in bulk; competition from MNC brands forced Indian television companies to move into assembling activities for MNCs, and even when they bought capacitors they preferred to import, as the imported item cost half of what people like Ravi charged. Ravi now produces less than half the capacitors he produced in 2000 and has only seven workers; many of his friends in the same business in Hyderabad and Chennai have closed their units.

Recent studies point out that small producers in India need three things to compete better: (a) better roads, power, water, raw materials, marketing and information network; (b) improvements and modernisation of technology; (c) timely availability of credit at reasonable interest rates.

Competition and Uncertain Employment

Globalisation and the pressure of competition have substantially changed the lives of workers. Faced with growing competition, most employers these days prefer to employ workers “flexibly”, which means that workers’ jobs are no longer secure.

Case study

A garment worker — Sushila: 35-year-old Sushila has spent many years as a worker in the garment export industry of Delhi. She was employed as a “permanent worker” entitled to health insurance, provident fund and overtime at a double rate, when her factory closed in the late 1990s. After searching for a job for six months she finally got one 30 km from where she lives. Even after working in this factory for several years she is a temporary worker and earns less than half of what she was earning earlier. She leaves home every morning, seven days a week, at 7:30 a.m. and returns at 10 p.m. A day off from work means no wage, and she has none of the benefits she used to get. Factories closer to her home have widely fluctuating orders and therefore pay even less.

How do the workers in the garment export industry bear this pressure of competition? Large MNCs in the garment industry in Europe and America order their products from Indian exporters. These MNCs, with worldwide networks, look for the cheapest goods to maximise profits. To get large orders, Indian exporters try hard to cut their own costs; as the cost of raw materials cannot be reduced, they try to cut labour costs. Where a factory earlier employed workers permanently, now it employs them only temporarily so that it does not have to pay them for the whole year. Workers also have to put in very long hours and work night shifts regularly during the peak season. Wages are low and workers are forced to work overtime to make both ends meet.

While this competition among garment exporters has allowed MNCs to make large profits, workers are denied their fair share of the benefits brought about by globalisation. The conditions described have become common to many industrial units and services in India. Most workers today are employed in the unorganised sector, and increasingly conditions of work in the organised sector have come to resemble the unorganised sector: workers in the organised sector such as Sushila no longer get the protection and benefits they enjoyed earlier.

The Struggle for a Fair Globalisation

The evidence indicates that not everyone has benefited from globalisation. People with education, skill and wealth have made the best use of the new opportunities; on the other hand, there are many people who have not shared the benefits. Since globalisation is now a reality, the question is how to make it more “fair”. Fair globalisation would create opportunities for all, and also ensure that the benefits of globalisation are shared better.

The government can play a major role in making this possible. Its policies must protect the interests, not only of the rich and the powerful, but of all the people in the country. For instance, the government can:

  • ensure that labour laws are properly implemented and workers get their rights;
  • support small producers to improve their performance till they become strong enough to compete;
  • if necessary, use trade and investment barriers;
  • negotiate at the WTO for “fairer rules”;
  • align with other developing countries with similar interests to fight against the domination of developed countries in the WTO.

In the past few years, massive campaigns and representation by people’s organisations have influenced important decisions relating to trade and investments at the WTO. This has demonstrated that people also can play an important role in the struggle for fair globalisation.

Summing up

Globalisation is the process of rapid integration of countries, happening through greater foreign trade and foreign investment. MNCs play a major role, looking for cheap production locations, so production is organised in complex ways. Technology, particularly IT, has played a big role in organising production across countries, and liberalisation of trade and investment has facilitated globalisation by removing barriers. At the international level the WTO has put pressure on developing countries to liberalise. While globalisation has benefited well-off consumers and producers with skill, education and wealth, many small producers and workers have suffered. Fair globalisation would create opportunities for all and ensure the benefits are shared better.

Flashcards

All key terms

Key terms and definitions
TermSimple explanation
Multinational corporation (MNC)A company that owns or controls production in more than one nation.
InvestmentMoney spent to buy assets such as land, building, machines and other equipment, in the hope of earning profits.
Foreign investmentInvestment made by MNCs in a country other than their own.
Foreign tradeTrade between countries; it lets producers reach beyond domestic markets and expands buyers’ choice.
Integration of marketsThe connecting of markets in different countries through trade, so that choice rises and prices of similar goods tend to equalise.
GlobalisationThe process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries.
Trade barrierA government restriction on foreign trade — a tax on imports, or a quota on the number of goods that may be imported.
QuotaA limit placed by the government on the number of goods that can be imported.
LiberalisationRemoving barriers or restrictions set by the government; India began this around 1991.
WTOWorld Trade Organisation — aims to liberalise international trade, sets rules for it and sees that they are obeyed; about 160 members.
Special Economic Zone (SEZ)An industrial zone with world-class facilities where companies setting up production units need not pay taxes for the first five years.
Flexible employmentHiring workers for short periods when work is heavy, instead of on a regular basis, to reduce labour costs.
ContainerA large standard box in which goods are placed so that they can be loaded intact onto ships, railways, planes and trucks, cutting port handling costs.
Fair globalisationGlobalisation that creates opportunities for all and ensures that the benefits are shared better.
Value chain / production chainThe division of a production process into small parts spread across countries — design in one, components in another, assembly in a third.

NCERT In-text Questions and Answers

The questions printed inside the chapter

These are the “Can you…” and activity questions that appear inside the chapter text. Model answers are based on the chapter itself.

1.

Complete the following statement to show how the production process in the garment industry is spread across countries: “The brand tag says ‘Made in Thailand’ but they are not Thai products. We dissect the manufacturing process and look for the best solution at each step. We are doing it globally. In making garments, the company may, for example, get cotton fibre from Korea, …”

Model answer

“…then have it spun into yarn in Thailand, woven and dyed in India, cut and stitched in Bangladesh or Vietnam, have the buttons and zips supplied from China, and finally sell the finished garment under its brand in the United States and Europe, with the design and marketing handled from its headquarters.” The point is that no single country makes the shirt; the production process is divided into small parts and spread across the globe.

2.

Would you say Ford Motors is an MNC? Why?

Model answer

Yes. An MNC is a company that owns or controls production in more than one nation, and Ford’s production is spread over 26 countries, with a plant in India near Chennai in collaboration with Mahindra and Mahindra.

3.

What is foreign investment? How much did Ford Motors invest in India?

Model answer

Foreign investment is investment — money spent on assets such as land, buildings, machines and equipment — made by an MNC in a country other than its own. Ford Motors invested Rs 1,700 crore to set up a large plant near Chennai.

4.

“By setting up their production plants in India, MNCs such as Ford Motors tap the advantage not only of the large markets that countries such as India provide, but also the lower costs of production.” Explain.

Model answer

India offers a large domestic market — 88,000 cars sold here by 2017 — so production can be sold locally without transport cost or import duty. At the same time, labour and other inputs are cheaper than in the US, so the same plant can also export 1,81,000 cars to South Africa, Mexico, Brazil and the USA at lower cost.

5.

Why do you think the company wants to develop India as a base for manufacturing car components for its global operations? Discuss: (a) cost of labour and other resources in India (b) the presence of several local manufacturers who supply auto-parts to Ford Motors (c) closeness to a large number of buyers in India and China.

Model answer

All three matter. (a) Cheaper labour and inputs lower the cost per component. (b) An existing network of local auto-part suppliers means components need not be imported, cutting cost and time. (c) India and China together are huge markets, so a base here serves both local assembly and regional demand — which is exactly how MNCs choose locations: close to markets, with cheap skilled and unskilled labour, and assured supplies.

6.

In what ways will the production of cars by Ford Motors in India lead to interlinking of production?

Model answer

Ford’s Indian plant buys components from local suppliers, employs Indian workers, exports cars and components to other countries, and is linked to the parent company’s design and supply chains. So production in India becomes part of a global chain, with parts, technology and finished vehicles moving across borders.

7.

In what ways is an MNC different from other companies?

Model answer

An MNC owns or controls production in more than one nation; it sets up factories or offices where labour and resources are cheap, buys up local companies, or places orders with small producers and sells their output under its own brand. An ordinary company produces mainly within one country.

8.

Nearly all major multinationals are American, Japanese or European, such as Nike, Coca-Cola, Pepsi, Honda and Nokia. Can you guess why?

Model answer

Because these countries industrialised early, accumulated large amounts of capital and technology, and their companies had the wealth to invest abroad and the brand power to sell globally. The chapter notes that many top MNCs have wealth exceeding the entire budgets of developing country governments.

9.

What was the main channel connecting countries in the past? How is it different now?

Model answer

In the past, trade was the main channel: raw material, foodstuff and finished products crossed borders while production stayed within countries. Now MNCs themselves organise production across countries — design in one, components in another, assembly in a third — so it is not only goods but production, investment and technology that move.

10.

Distinguish between foreign trade and foreign investment.

Model answer

Foreign trade is the exchange of goods and services between countries. Foreign investment is money spent by an MNC on assets — land, buildings, machines — in another country, in the hope of earning profits.

11.

In recent years China has been importing steel from India. Explain how the import of steel by China will affect (a) steel companies in China (b) steel companies in India (c) industries buying steel for production of other industrial goods in China.

Model answer

(a) Chinese steel companies face competition and may lose market share or cut prices. (b) Indian steel companies gain a large new market, higher sales and profits. (c) Chinese industries that use steel get it cheaper, lowering their costs — as Indian buyers gained from cheaper Chinese toys.

12.

How will the import of steel from India into the Chinese markets lead to integration of markets for steel in the two countries?

Model answer

With trade open, steel moves from one market to the other; Chinese buyers get more choice; prices of similar steel in the two markets tend to move closer together; and producers in both countries compete even though they are thousands of miles apart. That is what integration of markets means.

13.

What is the role of MNCs in the globalisation process?

Model answer

They are the main agents: they invest abroad, shift and interlink production, control a large part of foreign trade, and carry technology, capital and management across borders — so goods, services, investments and technology move between countries as never before.

14.

What are the various ways in which countries can be linked?

Model answer

Through movement of goods and services (trade), of investment and technology (MNCs), and of people (migration for better income, jobs or education) — and through communication that lets information move instantly.

15.

Choose the correct option: Globalisation, by connecting countries, shall result in (a) lesser competition among producers (b) greater competition among producers (c) no change in competition among producers.

Model answer

(b) greater competition among producers — as Indian toy makers discovered when Chinese toys entered the market.

16.

In the news magazine example, underline the words describing the use of technology in production. How is information technology connected with globalisation? Would globalisation have been possible without expansion of IT?

Model answer

The text, design orders and payments travel through the internet and telecommunication; designing is done on computers; the printed magazines are flown to London. IT connects globalisation because it allows information — text, sound and images — to be digitised and sent anywhere instantly at negligible cost, so work can be located wherever it is cheapest. Without IT, services could not have been spread across countries as they are now; globalisation would have been far more limited.

17.

What do you understand by liberalisation of foreign trade?

Model answer

It means removing the barriers and restrictions the government had placed on foreign trade and investment, so that businesses can decide freely what to import or export and foreign companies can set up factories and offices here. India began this around 1991.

18.

Tax on imports is one type of trade barrier. The government could also place a limit on the number of goods that can be imported — known as quotas. Explain, using the example of Chinese toys, how quotas can be used as trade barriers. Do you think this should be used? Discuss.

Model answer

If the government allows only, say, 10 lakh Chinese toys a year, importers can bring in no more than that, so supply is limited, prices stay high and Indian toy makers keep their market. A quota is therefore a barrier like a tax. Whether it should be used is debatable: it protects domestic producers and jobs, but it also raises prices and reduces choice for consumers, and may invite retaliation. It is best used temporarily while producers become competitive.

19.

Fill in the blanks: WTO was started at the initiative of ___ countries. The aim of the WTO is to ___. WTO establishes rules regarding ___ for all countries, and sees that ___. In practice, trade between countries is not ___. Developing countries like India have ___, whereas developed countries, in many cases, have continued to provide protection to their producers.

Model answer

developed; liberalise international trade; international trade; these rules are obeyed; free and fair; removed trade barriers.

20.

What do you think can be done so that trade between countries is more fair?

Model answer

Developed countries should also cut the subsidies and barriers they retain; WTO rules should apply equally to all; developing countries should negotiate jointly for fairer rules; and governments should support small producers until they can compete, while enforcing labour and environmental standards.

21.

In the example we saw that the US government gives massive sums of money to farmers for production. At times governments also give support to promote production of certain types of goods, such as those which are environmentally friendly. Discuss whether these are fair or not.

Model answer

Support that helps farmers adopt environment-friendly methods, or protects the poor, can be defended as serving a public purpose. Support that lets a rich country’s farmers sell below cost in other countries’ markets distorts trade and harms poorer farmers — that is unfair. The test is whether the support corrects a market failure or simply transfers advantage to those who already have it.

22.

How has competition benefited people in India?

Model answer

Consumers, particularly well-off urban consumers, have a greater choice of goods with improved quality and lower prices — cars, electronics, toys, garments — raising their standard of living. Competition also pushed Indian companies to invest in new technology and raise standards, and some have become multinationals themselves.

23.

Should more Indian companies emerge as MNCs? How would it benefit the people in the country?

Model answer

Yes, if they compete on quality. Indian MNCs earn foreign exchange, create jobs at home and abroad, bring in technology and give Indian workers and suppliers access to global markets. But the benefits depend on whether the gains are shared with workers and small suppliers.

24.

Why do governments try to attract more foreign investment?

Model answer

Because foreign investment brings capital, technology, management skills and jobs, and links the country to global production networks — hence SEZs with world-class facilities and tax holidays for the first five years, and flexibility in labour laws.

25.

The setting up of SEZs has been opposed by some people in India. Find out who these people are and why they are opposing it.

Model answer

Mainly farmers and villagers whose land is acquired for the zones, and workers’ groups who fear that the flexibility in labour laws will leave jobs insecure. Farmers lose land and livelihood, often with inadequate compensation, while workers lose the protection that organised sector laws gave them.

26.

What are the ways in which Ravi’s small production unit was affected by rising competition?

Model answer

After import restrictions on capacitors were removed in 2001, his main clients — television companies — either shifted to assembling for MNCs or imported capacitors at half his price. He now produces less than half of what he made in 2000 and employs seven workers instead of 20.

27.

Should producers such as Ravi stop production because their cost of production is higher compared to producers in other countries? What do you think?

Model answer

Not necessarily. Stopping would destroy jobs and skills; the better path is to become competitive — with better infrastructure, modern technology and affordable credit, which are the three things the chapter says small producers need. Government support during the transition, and protection where dumping occurs, can be justified.

28.

Recent studies point out that small producers in India need three things to compete better: (a) better roads, power, water, raw materials, marketing and information network (b) improvements and modernisation of technology (c) timely availability of credit at reasonable interest rates. How would these help? Do you think MNCs will be interested in investing in these? Do you think the government has a role?

Model answer

(a) Good infrastructure cuts costs and delivery time, so the product can compete on price. (b) Modern technology raises quality and productivity. (c) Cheap, timely credit lets producers invest and hold stock instead of selling cheap. MNCs will not usually invest in public infrastructure or in tiny units — they invest where such facilities already exist. That is precisely why the government has a role: it must build infrastructure, support technology upgradation and ensure credit reaches small producers.

29.

In what ways has competition affected workers, Indian exporters and foreign MNCs in the garment industry?

Model answer

MNCs gain large profits by playing exporters against one another to get the cheapest goods. Indian exporters get large orders but must cut costs, especially labour costs, to keep them. Workers lose: permanent jobs become temporary, hours lengthen, night shifts become regular, wages fall and benefits disappear — as in Sushila’s case.

30.

What can be done by each of the following so that workers get a fair share of the benefits of globalisation? (a) government (b) employers at the exporting factories (c) MNCs (d) workers.

Model answer

(a) Government: enforce labour laws, inspect workplaces, ensure minimum wages and social security. (b) Employers: pay fair wages, give written contracts, limit hours, provide safety and allow unions. (c) MNCs: adopt codes of conduct for suppliers, pay prices that allow decent wages and audit working conditions. (d) Workers: organise into unions and SHG-like bodies, know their rights and bargain collectively.

31.

One of the present debates in India is whether companies should have flexible policies for employment. Summarise the point of view of employers and workers.

Model answer

Employers argue that orders fluctuate, so they need to hire for short periods to keep costs low and remain competitive — otherwise they lose contracts to other countries. Workers argue that flexibility means insecurity: no contract, no leave, no provident fund, long hours and lower pay, with no share in the profits that their work creates. The chapter’s evidence — Sushila — supports the workers’ concern.

08

NCERT Exercise Questions and Answers

End-of-chapter exercises, projects and activities

NCERT Exercises

Reproduced from the exercise section of the chapter, with model answers. Word limits are the ones the textbook sets.

1.
NCERT exercise3 marks

What do you understand by globalisation? Explain in your own words.

Model answer

Globalisation is the process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries. It happens through greater foreign trade and foreign investment: MNCs set up or control production in many countries, goods and services, capital and technology move across borders, and markets in different countries become linked, so that producers everywhere compete with one another.

2.
NCERT exercise5 marks

What were the reasons for putting barriers to foreign trade and foreign investment by the Indian government? Why did it wish to remove these barriers?

Model answer

After Independence barriers were put up to protect domestic producers from foreign competition: industries were just coming up in the 1950s and 1960s, and competition from imports at that stage would not have allowed them to grow, so India allowed imports only of essential items such as machinery, fertilisers and petroleum. Around 1991 the government decided that Indian producers were ready to compete, and that competition would improve their performance and quality; powerful international organisations supported this. So barriers were largely removed — liberalisation — allowing goods to be imported and exported easily and foreign companies to set up factories and offices here.

3.
NCERT exercise3 marks

How would flexibility in labour laws help companies?

Model answer

It lets companies hire workers for short periods when there is intense pressure of work instead of employing them regularly all year, so the cost of labour falls and they can quote lower prices to MNC buyers and win export orders. The cost, however, is borne by workers, whose jobs become insecure and who lose benefits such as provident fund, paid leave and overtime.

4.
NCERT exercise5 marks

What are the various ways in which MNCs set up, control or produce in other countries?

Model answer

(i) By setting up production jointly with local companies — bringing money for investment and the latest technology. (ii) By buying up local companies and expanding production, as Cargill bought Parakh Foods. (iii) By placing orders with small producers and selling the output under their own brand names, controlling price, quality, delivery and labour conditions. (iv) By setting up their own factories and offices where markets are close, labour is cheap and other factors of production are assured.

5.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Why do developed countries want developing countries to liberalise their trade and investment? What do you think should the developing countries demand in return?

Model answer

Because liberalisation opens markets for their goods, services and capital, and lets their MNCs produce where costs are lowest. In return, developing countries should demand that developed countries also remove their own trade barriers and farm subsidies, that WTO rules apply equally to all, that labour and environmental standards are enforced, and that technology transfer and fair prices are guaranteed.

6.
NCERT exercise5 marks

“The impact of globalisation has not been uniform.” Explain this statement.

Model answer

Because the gains are unevenly shared. Well-off urban consumers gained greater choice, better quality and lower prices; MNCs gained from investing in India; top Indian companies gained from competition, new technology and even became multinationals; and IT services created new jobs. But small producers in batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys, tyres, dairy and edible oil were hit hard, with units shutting down and workers losing jobs, and workers in export industries such as garments lost permanent jobs, benefits and secure hours. People with education, skill and wealth made the best use of opportunities; many others did not share the benefits.

7.
NCERT exercise3 marks

How has liberalisation of trade and investment policies helped the globalisation process?

Model answer

By removing the barriers and restrictions the government had set, it allowed goods to be imported and exported easily, let foreign companies set up factories and offices in India, and allowed businesses to decide freely what to import or export. This increased foreign trade and foreign investment — the two channels through which countries become integrated.

8.
NCERT exercise3 marks

How does foreign trade lead to integration of markets across countries? Explain with an example other than those given here.

Model answer

With trade open, goods travel from one market to another, buyers get more choice, prices of similar goods in the two markets tend to equalise, and producers compete across borders. Example: Indian basmati rice sold in the Gulf and Iranian or Thai rice sold in India — buyers compare prices, and producers in all three countries must match quality and price, so the markets become one interconnected market for rice.

9.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Globalisation will continue in the future. Can you imagine what the world would be like twenty years from now? Give reasons for your answer.

Model answer

Model answer: production will be even more finely divided across countries, with design, manufacture, assembly and services located wherever costs and skills are best; digital services will be traded as goods are now; Indian companies will be multinationals in more sectors. But there will also be more resistance — demands for fair wages, environmental standards and protection of small producers — and possibly more restrictions on the movement of people. The reasons are the continuing fall in communication and transport costs, and the political pressure to make globalisation fairer.

10.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Supposing you find two people arguing: one is saying globalisation has hurt our country’s development, the other that it is helping India develop. How would you respond to these arguments?

Model answer

Both have part of the truth. Globalisation has helped: consumers have more choice at lower prices, MNC investment has created jobs in electronics, automobiles, food and banking, Indian firms have upgraded technology and some have become multinationals, and IT services earn foreign exchange. It has also hurt: small producers in capacitors, toys, tyres and dairy have shut down, and workers in export industries have lost secure jobs and benefits. So the real question is not whether globalisation is good or bad but how to make it fair — by enforcing labour laws, supporting small producers, negotiating fairer WTO rules and aligning with other developing countries.

11.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Fill in the blanks: Indian buyers have a greater choice of goods than they did two decades back. This is closely associated with the process of ___. Markets in India are selling goods produced in many other countries. This means there is increasing ___ with other countries. Moreover, the rising number of brands that we see in the markets might be produced by MNCs in India. MNCs are investing in India because ___. While consumers have more choices in the market, the effect of rising ___ and ___ has meant greater ___ among the producers.

Model answer

globalisation; integration (interconnection); MNCs invest because they can get cheap labour and other resources, close markets and favourable government policies; rising competition and imports have meant greater competition among producers.

12.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Match the following: (i) MNCs buy at cheap rates from small producers (ii) Quotas and taxes on imports are used to regulate trade (iii) Indian companies who have invested abroad (iv) IT has helped in spreading production of services (v) Several MNCs have invested in setting up factories in India for production — with (a) Automobiles (b) Garments, footwear, sports items (c) Call centres (d) Tata Motors, Infosys, Ranbaxy (e) Trade barriers.

Model answer

(i) → (b) garments, footwear, sports items; (ii) → (e) trade barriers; (iii) → (d) Tata Motors, Infosys, Ranbaxy; (iv) → (c) call centres; (v) → (a) automobiles.

13.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Choose the most appropriate option. (i) The past two decades of globalisation has seen rapid movements in: (a) goods, services and people between countries (b) goods, services and investments between countries (c) goods, investments and people between countries. (ii) The most common route for investments by MNCs in countries around the world is to: (a) set up new factories (b) buy existing local companies (c) form partnerships with local companies. (iii) Globalisation has led to improvement in living conditions: (a) of all the people (b) of people in the developed countries (c) of workers in the developing countries (d) none of the above.

Model answer

(i) (b) goods, services and investments between countries — movement of people has not increased much because of restrictions. (ii) (b) buy existing local companies. (iii) (d) none of the above — the impact has not been uniform; well-off consumers and skilled people gained, while many workers and small producers did not.

14.
NCERT projectProject

Additional activity — take some branded products that we use every day (soaps, toothpaste, garments, electronic goods) and check which are produced by MNCs.

Model answer

Look at the label for the manufacturer’s name and address, the “manufactured by / marketed by” line, and the country of origin. Many everyday brands are owned by MNCs even when made in Indian factories under licence. Record the brand, the owner company and its home country in a table. (Student activity.)

15.
NCERT projectProject

Additional project — take any Indian industry or service and collect information on: producers in the industry; whether the product is exported; whether MNCs are among the producers; competition; conditions of work; major changes in the last 15 years; problems people face.

Model answer

For example, the automobile industry: many producers (Maruti Suzuki, Hyundai, Tata, Mahindra, Toyota); exports are substantial; several are MNCs or joint ventures; competition is intense with frequent new models; conditions of work vary between organised plants and unorganised component suppliers; the major change since 1991 has been liberalisation, foreign entry and a shift to exports; problems include cost pressure on small component makers and job insecurity for contract workers. (Student project.)

09

Important Questions and Answers

Board-style practice

Practice questions

Written in the style of CBSE board papers. They are additional practice, not NCERT originals.

1.

What is an MNC? How does it spread production across countries? (5 marks)

Model answer

An MNC is a company that owns or controls production in more than one nation. It sets up offices and factories where it can get cheap labour and other resources, so that costs are low and profits greater. It may set up production jointly with a local company — bringing money for investment and the latest technology — or, most commonly, buy up local companies and expand, as Cargill bought Parakh Foods. It may also place orders with large numbers of small producers and sell their output under its own brand, controlling price, quality, delivery and labour conditions. In each case production is divided into small parts and spread across the globe, so production in dispersed locations becomes interlinked.

2.

Explain any three factors that have enabled globalisation. (5 marks)

Model answer

Technology — transport: improvements in transportation have made faster delivery over long distances possible at lower cost; containers allow goods to be loaded intact onto ships, railways, planes and trucks, hugely reducing port handling costs; the cost of air transport has fallen. Technology — information and communication: telecommunications, computers and the internet allow instant contact, access to information and the sending of digitised text, sound and images across the world at negligible cost, so services can be produced wherever it is cheapest. Liberalisation: the removal of barriers on foreign trade and foreign investment — in India from around 1991 — allowed goods to be imported and exported easily and foreign companies to set up factories here. The WTO has added international pressure to liberalise.

3.

What is a trade barrier? Why did India use them and why did it remove them? (5 marks)

Model answer

A trade barrier is any government restriction on foreign trade — a tax on imports, or a quota limiting the number that may be imported. India used them after Independence to protect domestic producers from foreign competition while industries were just coming up in the 1950s and 1960s, allowing imports only of essential items such as machinery, fertilisers and petroleum. Around 1991 the government decided that Indian producers should compete globally, believing competition would improve their performance and quality; powerful international organisations supported this. Barriers were therefore largely removed — liberalisation — so goods could be imported and exported easily and foreign companies could set up factories and offices here.

4.

How has globalisation affected small producers and workers in India? (5 marks)

Model answer

Small producers in batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys, tyres, dairy products and vegetable oil have been hit hard by competition; several units have shut down and workers have lost jobs — Ravi’s capacitor unit in Hosur now employs 7 instead of 20 and produces less than half of what it made in 2000. Small and medium industries employ 11 crore workers, next only to agriculture, so the effect is large. Workers face flexible employment: permanent jobs become temporary, hours lengthen, night shifts become regular, wages fall and benefits such as provident fund and health insurance disappear, as in Sushila’s case. Conditions in the organised sector increasingly resemble the unorganised sector, and workers are denied their fair share of the gains.

5.

What is fair globalisation? What can the government do to achieve it? (5 marks)

Model answer

Fair globalisation would create opportunities for all and ensure that its benefits are shared better. Since globalisation is a reality, the question is how to make it fair. The government can ensure that labour laws are properly implemented and workers get their rights; support small producers to improve their performance until they are strong enough to compete; use trade and investment barriers if necessary; negotiate at the WTO for fairer rules; and align with other developing countries with similar interests against the domination of developed countries in the WTO. Campaigns by people’s organisations have already influenced decisions at the WTO, showing that people can play an important role.

6.

Why is the WTO criticised by developing countries? (3 marks)

Model answer

Because although the WTO is supposed to allow free trade for all, in practice developed countries have unfairly retained trade barriers and continue to subsidise their farmers heavily — in the US, agriculture is only 1 per cent of GDP and 0.5 per cent of employment, yet receives massive support, so US farmers sell at abnormally low prices abroad. Meanwhile WTO rules have forced developing countries to remove their barriers. Developing countries ask whether this is free and fair trade.

7.

What are SEZs? Why are they opposed? (3 marks)

Model answer

Special Economic Zones are industrial zones set up to attract foreign companies, with world-class facilities — electricity, water, roads, transport, storage, and recreational and educational facilities — where companies need not pay taxes for the first five years. They are opposed by farmers and villagers whose land is acquired, often with inadequate compensation and loss of livelihood, and by workers’ groups who fear that flexibility in labour laws will make jobs insecure.

8.

How has competition affected consumers and Indian companies? (3 marks)

Model answer

Consumers, especially well-off urban consumers, have a wider choice of goods with improved quality and lower prices. Indian companies have been pushed to invest in new technology and production methods and to raise standards; some have gained from collaborations with foreign firms, and some — Tata Motors, Infosys, Ranbaxy, Asian Paints, Sundaram Fasteners — have become multinationals themselves.

9.

Explain the role of containers and IT in globalisation. (3 marks)

Model answer

Containers allow goods to be loaded intact onto ships, railways, planes and trucks, cutting port handling costs and speeding exports to markets. IT — telecommunications, computers and the internet — allows information, orders and payments to cross the world instantly at negligible cost, so a magazine for London readers can be designed and printed in Delhi, and call centres in India can serve customers abroad. Both lower the cost of doing business across borders.

10.

Why has the movement of people between countries not increased as much as the movement of goods and capital? (2 marks)

Model answer

Because of various restrictions — visa rules and immigration controls — that countries impose on the entry of people, even as they liberalise trade and investment.

10

Previous Year Questions (PYQs)

Asked in CBSE board exams

Previous year questions

These follow the pattern of questions set in CBSE Social Science papers for this chapter. Answers are model answers.

1.
CBSE pattern

What is globalisation? State any two ways in which MNCs interlink production across countries. (CBSE pattern, 3 marks)

Model answer

Globalisation is the process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries. MNCs interlink production by buying up local companies and expanding them, and by placing orders with large numbers of small producers and selling their output under their own brand names; they also set up joint ventures with local firms.

2.
CBSE pattern

Why did the Indian government remove barriers on foreign trade and investment around 1991? (3 marks)

Model answer

Because it decided that Indian producers were ready to compete with producers around the globe, and that competition would improve their performance and quality. The decision was supported by powerful international organisations such as the WTO.

3.
CBSE pattern

What is a trade barrier? Give one example. (2 marks)

Model answer

A government restriction on foreign trade used to regulate it — for example a tax on imports, or a quota limiting the quantity that may be imported.

4.
CBSE pattern

How have containers helped in globalisation? (2 marks)

Model answer

Containers let goods be loaded intact onto ships, railways, planes and trucks, which has led to a huge reduction in port handling costs and increased the speed with which exports reach markets.

5.
CBSE pattern

Explain the impact of globalisation on workers in the garment export industry. (3 marks)

Model answer

Permanent jobs have become temporary, working hours have lengthened, night shifts are regular in peak season, wages are low and benefits such as provident fund and health insurance have gone — as in Sushila’s case, where she earns less than half her earlier wage and works seven days a week.

6.
CBSE pattern

Why do MNCs set up production in countries where they can get cheap labour? (2 marks)

Model answer

Because cheap labour and other resources lower the cost of production, which raises the MNC’s profits — the chapter estimates that spreading production across countries can mean 50–60 per cent cost savings.

7.
CBSE pattern

What is foreign investment? (2 marks)

Model answer

Money spent by an MNC to buy assets such as land, buildings, machines and other equipment in another country, in the hope of earning profits.

8.
CBSE pattern

State two steps taken by the government of India to attract foreign investment. (2 marks)

Model answer

Setting up Special Economic Zones with world-class facilities where companies pay no taxes for the first five years; and allowing flexibility in labour laws so that companies can hire workers for short periods.

9.
CBSE pattern

How has globalisation benefited well-off consumers in India? (2 marks)

Model answer

They have a much greater choice of goods, with improved quality and lower prices for many products, and therefore a higher standard of living than was possible earlier.

10.
CBSE pattern

What is meant by fair globalisation? (2 marks)

Model answer

Globalisation that creates opportunities for all and ensures that its benefits are shared better — rather than benefiting only those with education, skill and wealth.

11

Frequently Asked Questions

Quick clarifications

1.

Is globalisation the same as liberalisation?

Model answer

No. Liberalisation is the removal of government barriers on trade and investment; it is one of the causes that has enabled globalisation, the broader process of countries becoming integrated.

2.

What is the difference between foreign trade and foreign investment?

Model answer

Foreign trade is the exchange of goods and services across borders; foreign investment is money spent by an MNC on assets in another country.

3.

Why do MNCs not always build new factories?

Model answer

Because buying an existing local company is quicker and brings a ready brand, network and plant — as Cargill gained Parakh Foods’ four refineries and marketing network.

4.

Has the movement of people increased with globalisation?

Model answer

Not much. There are various restrictions on migration, so while goods, services, investment and technology move more freely, people do not.

5.

Who loses from cheap imports?

Model answer

Domestic producers in that product — Indian toy makers, capacitor makers like Ravi — and their workers, who may lose jobs or income. Consumers gain.

6.

Is the WTO a world government?

Model answer

No. It is an organisation of about 160 member countries that sets rules for international trade and monitors them; it cannot by itself force a country to change its laws, though it applies strong pressure.

7.

Why are farm subsidies an issue at the WTO?

Model answer

Because developed countries subsidise their farmers heavily and still ask developing countries to remove trade barriers, which lets subsidised produce be sold cheaply abroad and hurt farmers in poorer countries.

8.

What does “flexible employment” mean?

Model answer

Hiring workers for short periods when work is heavy rather than employing them regularly, so that the employer avoids paying wages, benefits and social security all year.

12

Assertion-Reason Questions

Choose the correct option

How to answer

(a) Both A and R are true and R explains A. (b) Both are true but R does not explain A. (c) A is true, R is false. (d) A is false, R is true.

1.

Assertion (A): An MNC owns or controls production in more than one nation.
Reason (R): MNCs set up factories where labour and other resources are cheap.

2.

Assertion (A): Foreign trade integrates markets across countries.
Reason (R): With trade open, prices of similar goods in two markets tend to become equal.

3.

Assertion (A): Globalisation has benefited everyone equally.
Reason (R): The impact of globalisation has not been uniform.

4.

Assertion (A): Containers have reduced port handling costs.
Reason (R): Goods can be loaded intact onto ships, railways, planes and trucks.

5.

Assertion (A): India removed most trade barriers around 1991.
Reason (R): It wanted Indian producers to compete globally and improve quality.

6.

Assertion (A): The WTO has forced developed countries to remove their farm subsidies.
Reason (R): Developed countries have unfairly retained trade barriers.

7.

Assertion (A): SEZs offer tax exemption for the first five years.
Reason (R): They are meant to attract foreign companies to invest in India.

8.

Assertion (A): Small producers have gained from globalisation.
Reason (R): Several small units in batteries, capacitors and toys have shut down.

9.

Assertion (A): Workers in the organised sector now enjoy greater security than before.
Reason (R): Employers increasingly prefer to hire workers flexibly for short periods.

10.

Assertion (A): Fair globalisation requires government action.
Reason (R): Government can enforce labour laws, support small producers and negotiate fairer WTO rules.

Source-Based and Case-Based Questions

Read the passage or table, then answer

Source 1 — Ford Motors in India

Source extract

Ford Motors, an American company, is one of the world’s largest automobile manufacturers with production spread over 26 countries of the world. Ford Motors came to India in 1995 and spent Rs 1,700 crore to set up a large plant near Chennai. This was done in collaboration with Mahindra and Mahindra, a major Indian manufacturer of jeeps and trucks. By the year 2017, Ford Motors was selling 88,000 cars in the Indian markets, while another 1,81,000 cars were exported from India to South Africa, Mexico, Brazil and United States of America. In recent years, Ford Company stopped producing cars for selling in India but export cars and car engines on a small scale to other countries.

1.

Is Ford Motors an MNC? Give the evidence from the passage.

Model answer

Yes — its production is spread over 26 countries, and it owns a plant in India near Chennai, which is production in more than one nation.

2.

How much foreign investment did Ford bring, and with whom did it collaborate?

Model answer

Rs 1,700 crore, in collaboration with Mahindra and Mahindra.

3.

What advantage did India offer Ford? Use the numbers in the passage.

Model answer

A large domestic market (88,000 cars sold) and lower production costs, which made it worthwhile to also export 1,81,000 cars to South Africa, Mexico, Brazil and the USA — so India served both as a market and an export base.

Source 2 — Ravi’s capacitor unit

Case study

Ravi took a loan from the bank to start his own company producing capacitors in 1992 in Hosur, an industrial town in Tamil Nadu. Capacitors are used in many electronic home appliances including tube lights, television etc. Within three years, he was able to expand production and had 20 workers working under him. His struggle to run his company started when the government removed restrictions on imports of capacitors as per its agreement at WTO in 2001. His main clients, the television companies, used to buy different components including capacitors in bulk for the manufacture of television sets. However, competition from the MNC brands forced the Indian television companies to move into assembling activities for MNCs. Even when some of them bought capacitors, they would prefer to import as the price of the imported item was half the price charged by people like Ravi. Ravi now produces less than half the capacitors that he produced in the year 2000 and has only seven workers working for him.

1.

What event started Ravi’s difficulties, and why?

Model answer

The removal of import restrictions on capacitors in 2001 under India’s WTO commitment. Imported capacitors cost half of what he charged, so his buyers switched to imports.

2.

How did the change in his clients’ business affect him?

Model answer

His main clients, television companies, were forced by MNC competition into assembling for MNCs, which reduced their need for his components and made them prefer cheap imports.

3.

What does Ravi’s case show about the impact of globalisation?

Model answer

That its impact is not uniform: consumers got cheaper televisions, but a small producer lost half his output and two-thirds of his workers — the “compete or perish” problem the chapter describes.

Source 3 — Debate on trade practices at the WTO

Source extract

Developing countries are asking the developed country governments, “We have reduced trade barriers as per WTO rules. But you have ignored the rules of WTO and have continued to pay your farmers vast sums of money. You have asked our governments to stop supporting our farmers, but you are doing so yourselves. Is this free and fair trade?”

Compare this to a developed country such as the US with the share of agriculture in GDP at 1% and its share in total employment a tiny 0.5%! And yet this very small percentage of people who are engaged in agriculture in the US receive massive sums of money from the US government for production and for exports to other countries.

1.

What is the developing countries’ complaint?

Model answer

That the rules are applied unequally: they removed their trade barriers as the WTO required, while developed countries kept paying their farmers vast sums and so retained an unfair advantage.

2.

How do US subsidies affect farmers in developing countries?

Model answer

Subsidised US farmers can sell at abnormally low prices, and the surplus is sold in other countries’ markets at low prices, undercutting local farmers and reducing their incomes.

3.

What does the passage suggest developing countries should do?

Model answer

Negotiate jointly at the WTO for fairer rules and align with other developing countries with similar interests — which is what the chapter recommends in “the struggle for a fair globalisation”.

This chapter sets no map work. Instead, draw a flow chart of the production of a shirt across four countries and mark what each country contributes.

For example: cotton fibre from Korea → yarn spun in Thailand → woven and dyed in India → cut and stitched in Bangladesh → buttons from China → sold under an MNC brand in the USA and Europe, with design and marketing at the MNC’s headquarters.

2.

Draw a table classifying the effects of globalisation into “gains” and “losses” for four groups: consumers, MNCs, Indian large companies, small producers and workers.

Model answer

Consumers: gains (choice, quality, lower prices), losses (little for well-off consumers). MNCs: gains (profits, market access). Indian large companies: gains (technology, exports, becoming MNCs), losses (competition). Small producers and workers: losses (closures, job insecurity, lower wages).

3.

On a sketch map of India, mark Chennai (Ford plant), Hosur (Ravi’s unit), Delhi (Sushila’s garment factory) and Ludhiana (footballs for MNCs).

Model answer

Chennai in Tamil Nadu, Hosur also in Tamil Nadu near Bengaluru, Delhi in the north, Ludhiana in Punjab. Each is an example of production linked to global chains.

17

HOTS and Competency-Based Questions

Think beyond the text

Higher order thinking

These ask you to apply, compare or evaluate. Model answers are indicative — your own well-reasoned answer can differ.

1.

“Globalisation is fun” says the businessman in the cartoon; “That’s our world you’re playing with” says the girl. Whose view does the chapter finally support, and why?

Model answer

The chapter supports neither extreme. It records real gains — greater choice, lower prices, new jobs, Indian companies becoming multinationals — and real losses — small producers shut out, workers made insecure. Its conclusion is that globalisation is a reality, so the task is to make it fair: opportunities for all and benefits shared better, through enforced labour laws, support to small producers, trade rules that apply equally, and negotiation at the WTO. The girl’s warning about consequences is taken seriously. (Model answer.)

2.

Why can a country gain from trade in the short run and lose in the long run? Use the toys and capacitors examples.

Model answer

In the short run consumers gain from cheaper, better-designed imports — toys became cheaper and 70–80 per cent of shops switched. But if domestic producers such as Ravi’s capacitor unit shut down, capacity and skills are lost, jobs disappear, and the country becomes dependent on imports whose prices and supply it does not control. The long-run loss is the destruction of productive capability that is hard to rebuild. This is why the chapter argues for supporting small producers until they can compete. (Model answer.)

3.

Should India offer even more flexibility in labour laws to attract foreign investment? Argue both sides and conclude.

Model answer

For: flexible hiring lowers costs and helps win export orders, which create jobs and foreign exchange; countries compete for investment. Against: flexibility means temporary contracts, long hours, no provident fund or health cover, and conditions in the organised sector coming to resemble the unorganised sector — as Sushila’s case shows; insecure workers are also less productive and less able to invest in skills. Conclusion: investment should be attracted through infrastructure, power, credit and skills rather than by lowering protection; where flexibility is allowed, a basic floor of wages, safety and social security should remain. (Model answer.)

4.

A garment exporter says, “We cannot raise wages; the MNC will go to Bangladesh.” Is that a good argument? What could change the outcome?

Model answer

It is a real constraint — MNCs do look for the cheapest source — but it is not a complete argument, because it treats the wage as the only variable. Costs also depend on productivity, delivery reliability, infrastructure and design capability, and buyers increasingly care about labour standards. Outcomes change if exporters upgrade technology and skills, if the government improves power and transport, and if MNCs adopt and audit supplier codes of conduct. Collective bargaining across a region can also prevent a race to the bottom. (Model answer.)

5.

Why is the movement of goods freer than the movement of people? Is that fair?

Model answer

Because trade and investment liberalisation were pushed by international organisations and by MNCs that benefit from moving goods and capital, while migration is controlled by national visa and immigration laws that reflect security, labour-market and political concerns. Whether it is fair is contested: developing countries that export labour argue that if capital can move freely, labour should too, while receiving countries argue that unmanaged migration creates social and wage pressures. The chapter simply notes that movement of people has not increased much because of restrictions. (Model answer.)

6.

Design three policies that would make globalisation fairer for Indian small producers, and say who would oppose each.

Model answer

(i) Cheap, timely institutional credit and technology upgradation support for small units — opposed by those who fear fiscal cost and by large firms that prefer less competition. (ii) Strict enforcement of labour and environmental standards in export units — opposed by some exporters who fear losing orders, though supported by workers. (iii) Joint negotiation with other developing countries at the WTO against farm subsidies and non-tariff barriers — opposed by developed-country farm lobbies. A good answer explains the trade-off for each. (Model answer.)
