Quick Revision Sheet

One page before the exam

Production across countries

  • MNC = owns/controls production in more than one nation.
  • Sets up where markets are close, labour cheap, other factors assured, policies favourable.
  • Routes: joint ventures, buying local firms (Cargill–Parakh), orders to small producers under own brand.
  • 50–60% cost savings possible. Ford: 1995, Rs 1,700 crore, Chennai, 26 countries.

Foreign trade

  • Creates markets beyond home country; expands buyers’ choice.
  • Chinese toys: 70–80% of shops switched in a year; prices fell; Indian toy makers lost.
  • Integration of markets: choice rises, prices of similar goods equalise, producers compete.

Globalisation

  • Rapid integration/interconnection between countries.
  • Enabled by transport technology (containers, cheaper air freight), IT (telecom, computers, internet), and liberalisation.
  • Movement of people has not increased much because of restrictions.

Policy

  • Trade barrier = tax or quota. India used barriers after Independence to protect infant industries.
  • 1991: liberalisation — barriers largely removed; supported by international organisations.
  • WTO: about 160 members, started by developed countries; rules favour developed countries in practice.

Impact

  • Consumers: choice, quality, lower prices (well-off urban mainly).
  • MNCs: profits; jobs in phones, autos, electronics, food, banking.
  • Indian firms: technology, collaborations; Tata Motors, Infosys, Ranbaxy, Asian Paints, Sundaram Fasteners became MNCs.
  • Small producers hit: batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys, tyres, dairy, oil; 11 crore workers in small/medium industry.
  • Workers: flexible hiring, temporary contracts, long hours, lower pay — Sushila.

Fair globalisation

  • Opportunities for all; benefits shared better.
  • Government: enforce labour laws, support small producers, use barriers if needed, negotiate at WTO, align with developing countries.
  • SEZs: world-class facilities, no taxes for 5 years; opposed over land acquisition and labour flexibility.
19

Chapter Summary

The whole chapter in a few paragraphs

Until the middle of the twentieth century production was largely organised within countries, and trade was the main channel connecting them. Then multinational corporations — companies that own or control production in more than one nation — began to set up offices and factories where labour and resources are cheap, so that costs fall and profits rise. They work through joint ventures with local companies, by buying local firms (Cargill bought Parakh Foods), or by placing orders with small producers and selling the output under their own brands. Production is divided into small parts and spread across the globe, and widely dispersed production becomes interlinked.

Foreign trade lets producers reach beyond domestic markets and gives buyers more choice; with trade, prices of similar goods in different markets tend to equalise and producers compete across borders, so markets become integrated. Globalisation is this process of rapid integration between countries, enabled by improvements in transport — notably containers and cheaper air freight — by information and communication technology that lets information, orders and payments cross the world instantly, and by liberalisation of foreign trade and investment, which India began around 1991 after decades of protection. The WTO, with about 160 members, pushes for free trade but is criticised because developed countries retain barriers and farm subsidies while developing countries are pressed to remove theirs.

The impact has not been uniform. Consumers, especially well-off urban ones, gained greater choice, better quality and lower prices; MNCs gained profits; several Indian companies upgraded technology and some became multinationals; IT services created new jobs. But small producers in batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys, tyres, dairy and edible oil were hit hard, with closures and job losses, and workers face flexible employment — temporary contracts, long hours and lower pay — so that organised sector conditions increasingly resemble the unorganised sector. Fair globalisation would create opportunities for all and ensure benefits are shared better: governments must enforce labour laws, support small producers, use trade and investment barriers where needed, and negotiate fairer rules at the WTO together with other developing countries.
